question: What two mistakes do studies show most crash-involved riders make regarding braking and swerving?
choice_a: Underbraking the front tire and overbraking the rear, or not choosing to swerve when it was appropriate
choice_b: Overbraking the front and never using the rear brake at all
choice_c: Always swerving instead of braking, even when braking was better
choice_d: Using both brakes evenly at all times
explanation: Studies show most crash-involved riders underbrake the front tire and overbrake the rear, or did not separate braking from swerving, or did not choose swerving when it was appropriate.

question: To stop quickly, what should a rider do if the front wheel locks during braking?
choice_a: Keep the front brake locked and steer around the hazard
choice_b: Release the front brake lever immediately, then reapply it firmly
choice_c: Switch entirely to the rear brake for the remainder of the stop
explanation: To stop quickly, apply both brakes at the same time; if the front wheel locks, release the front brake lever immediately then reapply it firmly, while pressing down on the rear brake.

question: According to the manual, can a rider keep the rear wheel locked during a quick stop on good traction?
choice_a: No, a locked rear wheel always causes an immediate crash
choice_b: Only if the front wheel is also locked
choice_c: Yes, if it is upright and going in a straight line, you can control the motorcycle even with a locked rear wheel
explanation: If you accidentally lock the rear brake on a good traction surface, you can keep it locked until you have completely stopped; even with a locked rear wheel, you can control the motorcycle if it is upright and going straight.

question: If a rider must stop quickly while in a curve and cannot straighten the handlebars first, what should they do?
choice_a: Apply maximum brake force immediately regardless of lean angle
choice_b: Release both brakes and coast until upright
choice_c: Accelerate out of the curve before braking
choice_d: Brake smoothly and gradually, using less braking force than if the motorcycle were upright
explanation: If conditions do not allow straightening first, brake smoothly and gradually, but do not apply as much braking force as you would if the motorcycle were straight up, since less traction is available while leaned over.
source_note: CT Motorcycle Operator Manual, 'Stopping Quickly in a Curve'

question: What should a rider always do in the last few feet of stopping in a curve, per the manual?
choice_a: Straighten the handlebars to maintain balance and remain upright
choice_b: Keep the handlebars turned to hold the lean angle
explanation: Always straighten the handlebars in the last few feet of stopping to maintain your balance and remain upright.
source_note: CT Motorcycle Operator Manual, 'Stopping Quickly in a Curve'

question: What is a swerve, as defined in the manual?
choice_a: A gradual, wide turn made over several seconds
choice_b: A sudden change in direction, done by applying hand pressure to the handgrip on the side of the intended escape direction
choice_c: A full stop followed by a U-turn
choice_d: Using only the rear brake to change lanes
explanation: A swerve is a sudden change in direction. Apply a small amount of hand pressure to the handgrip on the side of your intended direction of escape, causing the motorcycle to lean quickly.
source_note: CT Motorcycle Operator Manual, 'Swerving or Turning Quickly'

question: When swerving, what should a rider do with braking, if the situation allows?
choice_a: Always brake and swerve at the exact same instant
choice_b: Braking should never be combined with swerving under any circumstances, even sequentially
choice_c: Separate braking from swerving -- brake before or after, never while making an aggressive swerve
choice_d: Only the rear brake should be used during a swerve
explanation: If the situation allows, separate braking from swerving. Brake before or after -- never while making an aggressive swerve.
source_note: CT Motorcycle Operator Manual, 'Swerving or Turning Quickly'

question: During a swerve, what should a rider keep their knees and feet doing?
choice_a: Lift feet off the footrests for balance
choice_b: Lean the body sharply while keeping the motorcycle vertical
choice_c: Stand up fully off the seat
choice_d: Keep knees against the tank and feet solidly on the footrests while the body stays upright and the motorcycle leans
explanation: Keep your body upright and allow the motorcycle to lean in the direction of the turn while keeping your knees against the tank and your feet solidly on the footrests.
source_note: CT Motorcycle Operator Manual, 'Swerving or Turning Quickly'

question: What is required to achieve maximum straight-line braking?
choice_a: Fully applying both front and rear brakes without locking either wheel
choice_b: Using only the front brake at full force
choice_c: Using only the rear brake at full force
choice_d: Locking both wheels simultaneously for the shortest stop
explanation: Maximum straight-line braking is accomplished by fully applying front and rear brakes without locking either wheel, while keeping the body centered and looking well ahead.
source_note: CT Motorcycle Operator Manual, 'Maximum Straight-Line Braking'

question: What immediately happens if the front wheel locks up and the brake lever is not fully released right away?
choice_a: Nothing serious; the motorcycle will continue to steer normally
choice_b: It will result in a crash, since front-wheel skids cause immediate loss of steering control and balance
choice_c: The rear wheel will automatically compensate
choice_d: The motorcycle will simply slow down faster with no downside
explanation: Front-wheel skids result in immediate loss of steering control and balance. Failure to fully release the brake lever immediately will result in a crash.

question: What is a 'high-side' crash, as described in the manual?
choice_a: A crash that only happens when riding uphill
choice_b: A crash caused exclusively by front tire failure
choice_c: When a misaligned, locked rear wheel is released and the motorcycle abruptly snaps upright, throwing the rider into the air
choice_d: A minor low-speed tip-over in a parking lot
explanation: If the rear wheel is out of alignment with the front and a locked rear wheel is released, the motorcycle can abruptly snap upright, throwing the rider into the air ahead of the motorcycle's path -- even slight misalignment can cause a high-side crash.

question: What is a primary cause of single-vehicle motorcycle crashes, per the manual?
choice_b: Tire pressure that is too high
choice_d: Motorcyclists running wide in a curve or turn
explanation: A primary cause of single-vehicle crashes is motorcyclists running wide in a curve or turn; every curve is different, so riders should be alert to whether it stays constant, widens, tightens, or has multiple turns.

question: Where does the manual recommend positioning yourself before entering a curve, to spot approaching traffic sooner?
choice_a: Move to the center of your lane before entering the curve and stay there until you exit
choice_b: Hug the outside edge of the curve at all times
choice_c: Ride in the oncoming lane briefly for a better view
choice_d: It does not matter where you position yourself in a curve
explanation: A good choice is to move to the center of your lane before entering a curve and stay there until you exit; this permits you to spot approaching traffic as soon as possible.

question: What does the manual say about following a fixed path through every curve?
choice_a: The exact same line should be used through every curve regardless of conditions
choice_b: Your best path may not always follow the curve of the road, and lane position should change with traffic and conditions
choice_c: Riders should always hug the inside line through every curve
choice_d: Curve position should never change once chosen
explanation: Your best path may not always follow the curve of the road. Change lane position depending on traffic, road conditions, and the curve of the road.

question: Why is it important to know when to swerve rather than only brake, according to the manual?
choice_a: Swerving is always safer than braking in every situation
choice_b: Braking is illegal in emergency situations
choice_c: It is not always desirable or possible to stop quickly, so riders must also be able to swerve around an obstacle
choice_d: Swerving is only taught for three-wheel motorcycles
explanation: It is not always desirable or possible to stop quickly to avoid an obstacle. Riders must also be able to swerve around an obstacle, and determining which skill is necessary for the situation is important.

question: When leaning a motorcycle in a curve, what happens to the amount of traction available for braking?
choice_a: It increases the more the motorcycle leans
choice_b: Lean angle has no effect on available traction
choice_c: Traction is only affected by tire pressure, not lean angle
choice_d: It is reduced, and the greater the lean angle, the more likely the tires are to lose traction
explanation: Any time a motorcycle is leaned over, the amount of traction available for braking is reduced. The greater the lean angle, the more the possibility of the tires losing traction.
source_note: CT Motorcycle Operator Manual, 'Braking in a Corner'

question: When must a rear-wheel-locked skid be released, if the rear wheel is out of alignment with the front?
choice_a: To regain control the brake must be released, but there is a risk of a high-side crash when this is done
choice_b: It should never be released once locked
choice_c: Releasing it has no risk under any conditions
choice_d: Only the front brake needs to be released, not the rear
explanation: As soon as the rear wheel locks, your ability to change direction is lost. To regain control, the brake must be released -- however, if the rear wheel is out of alignment with the front, there is a risk of a high-side crash.
